title: Wangari Maathai and the Seedlings Women Were Paid to Keep Alive
conflicts: First planting: the Green Belt Movement's own account (Goldman Prize guest post) says seven seedlings on World Environment Day 1977; the Nobel Committee chairman's 2004 presentation speech says nine trees in her backyard on 5 June 1977. The story gives both with who said what; Kamukunji Park (from her memoir via secondary pages that were blocked or dead) is not named. Tree totals: over 20 million by 1993 (women's reports, Right Livelihood; Nobel biography), about 30 million by 2004 (Nobel lecture, presentation speech, UB 2007), over 51 million by 2017 (the movement); each given with date and source. The presentation speech also says she resigned her chair in 1977, which the Nobel biography does not support; omitted.
notes: No loading source gives the payment amount per seedling, so none is stated; payment is described as for seedlings raised successfully (UB Reporter paraphrase) and as women's groups selling seedlings to the movement (Right Livelihood). Several Maathai quotations come from the UB Reporter's account of her 2007 lecture. The drought-killed first nursery is from America Magazine's review of Unbowed and attributed to the memoir.
